subject: Re: Dedicated SLA clarity + how priority lanes interact with reserved capacity
body:
From: Maya Chen <maya.chen@northwindhealth.ai>
To: Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwoodinference.com>
Cc: Liam O'Rourke <liam.orourke@redwoodinference.com>, Alex Rivera <alex.rivera@northwindhealth.ai>
Date: Tue, Jan 14, 2025 at 9:12 AM
Subject: Dedicated SLA clarity + how priority lanes interact with reserved capacity

Hi Lauren,

We’re reviewing the Dedicated order form + SLA language with our legal/procurement team.

Two questions we’d like to clarify in writing:

1) When you refer to “enterprise priority lanes” / “priority routing,” does that apply to Dedicated capacity as well, or only to the shared Hosted API fleet?

2) If priority lanes exist globally, can another customer’s burst impact our Dedicated latency/availability SLOs (e.g., shared control plane, shared routing layer, etc.)?

We’re trying to understand what isolation we get with Dedicated, and what behaviors to expect if we exceed our reserved throughput (429s vs queuing, Retry-After semantics, etc.).

Thanks,
Maya

—
Maya Chen
Director of Platform Engineering
Northwind Health



From: Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwoodinference.com>

Subject: Fwd: Dedicated SLA clarity + how priority lanes interact with reserved capacity

Forwarding from Northwind (Dedicated deal). They’re asking:

- whether enterprise priority lanes apply to Dedicated vs only shared Hosted
- whether other customers can impact Dedicated SLOs (routing/control plane shared components)
- expected behavior when they exceed reserved throughput (429 vs queueing, Retry-After)

Can you sanity check the correct technical + SRE wording? I want to respond today/tomorrow with something we can stand behind (and that matches current hot-route protection semantics).

Context: they’ll run 2 “hot” routes (chat + rerank) and are sensitive to tail latency. They also have spiky traffic during shift changes.

Thanks,
Lauren

Lauren Bishop
Product, Dedicated & Enterprise
Redwood Inference



From: Sean Gallagher <sean.gallagher@redwoodinference.com>
To: Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwoodinference.com>
Cc: Rafael Mendes <rafael.mendes@redwoodinference.com>, Nikhil Sharma <nikhil.sharma@redwoodinference.com>, Liam O'Rourke <liam.orourke@redwoodinference.com>
Date: Tue, Jan 14, 2025 at 11:01 AM
Subject: Re: Fwd: Dedicated SLA clarity + how priority lanes interact with reserved capacity

Here’s the SRE-safe framing:

- Dedicated = capacity isolation at the GPU pool / router lane level. Another customer’s burst should not consume your reserved GPUs.
- Priority lanes are primarily for the multi-tenant Hosted fleet (protect enterprise traffic vs self-serve). For Dedicated, the “enterprise lane” concept is not about competing with other tenants; it’s used for admission control/backpressure and predictable overload behavior.
- Shared components caveat: there is still a shared control plane + some shared routing infrastructure, but Dedicated dataplane scheduling is isolated. In practice, the main correlated risks are:
  - control plane outages affecting config propagation / deploys
  - regional networking events
  - global incidents that affect request admission at the edge (rare)
  These are captured in the availability SLA language; but other tenants’ traffic is not.
- Exceeding reserved throughput: we should prefer immediate 429 (or 503 in some failure modes) with Retry-After rather than deep queuing that blows up tail latency. That’s consistent with hot-route capacity protection direction.

If you want a single sentence for #2: “No, other customers’ load doesn’t steal Dedicated capacity; priority routing is to protect you from shared-fleet overload and provide clear over-capacity behavior when you exceed your own reservation.”

Rafael can add specifics on current headers/reason codes if you want.

Sean



From: Nikhil Sharma <nikhil.sharma@redwoodinference.com>
To: Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwoodinference.com>
Cc: Sean Gallagher <sean.gallagher@redwoodinference.com>, Rafael Mendes <rafael.mendes@redwoodinference.com>, Liam O'Rourke <liam.orourke@redwoodinference.com>
Date: Tue, Jan 14, 2025 at 12:26 PM
Subject: Re: Fwd: Dedicated SLA clarity + how priority lanes interact with reserved capacity

+1 to Sean’s summary.

Product wording suggestion (to keep this aligned with docs / not over-promise):

- “Priority lanes” is overloaded language. For Hosted API, it means tier-aware fairness across tenants.
- For Dedicated, the customer effectively has a private tier already. What we’re building under the hood (hot-route protection) will still enforce per-route limits and return standardized over-capacity responses (429 + Retry-After) so they can build sane client retry/backoff.

We can also explicitly state that:

- Dedicated customers can optionally configure per-route limits (by endpoint) to prevent runaway clients from taking down their own pool.
- If they need a hard reserved throughput number per route (e.g., chat must always get X req/s), we treat that as a sizing/policy config conversation, not an SLA default.

If helpful, I can attach the 1-pager language we’ve been using to explain priority lanes.

Nikhil



From: Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwoodinference.com>
To: Sean Gallagher <sean.gallagher@redwoodinference.com>, Nikhil Sharma <nikhil.sharma@redwoodinference.com>

Subject: Re: Fwd: Dedicated SLA clarity + how priority lanes interact with reserved capacity

Thanks both. Drafting a response to Maya below — please mark up if anything is off.

---

Maya — great questions. A few clarifications:

1) Priority lanes / priority routing: this mechanism is primarily for our multi-tenant Hosted API fleet to ensure enterprise traffic is protected during shared-fleet overload. For Dedicated, you already have isolated capacity (a reserved GPU pool) so other tenants’ traffic does not contend with your reservation.

2) Can other customers’ burst impact your Dedicated SLOs? Other tenants cannot “steal” Dedicated GPU capacity. There are shared platform components (edge admission, control plane/config) but the Dedicated dataplane capacity and scheduling is isolated. In practice, the most likely correlated risks are regional networking/cloud events or a control-plane incident; those are the types of issues covered under the general availability SLA.

3) If you exceed reserved throughput: our default behavior is to return an over-capacity response (HTTP 429) with Retry-After guidance rather than queueing indefinitely (which tends to create tail latency spikes). We can also configure per-route limits/guardrails so a single hot route or client can’t starve the rest of your traffic.

Happy to jump on a quick call if it’s easier — and we can also share the current Dedicated SLA PDF and a short explainer on the priority lane behavior.

---

Open question for you both: should I mention reason codes/headers explicitly (request-id + Retry-After) or keep it high-level?

Lauren

Subject: Re: Fwd: Dedicated SLA clarity + how priority lanes interact with reserved capacity

Draft looks good.

I’d keep reason codes out of email unless they asked for exact payloads. But it’s safe to say:

- 429 includes a request id
- Retry-After header where applicable

One tweak: in #2, “covered under the general availability SLA” is fine, but avoid implying control-plane incidents are excluded/included beyond what the SLA says. Maybe: “captured in the SLA availability definition” rather than “covered”.

Sean

Hi Maya,

Thanks — great questions. Clarifying a few points:

1) Priority lanes / priority routing: this is primarily a protection mechanism for the multi-tenant Hosted API fleet (so enterprise traffic is protected during shared-fleet overload). For Dedicated, you already have isolated capacity (a reserved GPU pool), so other tenants’ traffic does not contend with your reservation.

2) Can another customer’s burst impact Dedicated SLOs? Other tenants cannot “steal” Dedicated GPU capacity. There are shared platform components (e.g., edge admission, control plane/config), but Dedicated dataplane capacity and scheduling is isolated. The remaining shared-component risks are the kinds of issues described in the SLA availability definition (e.g., regional/network events, etc.).

3) If you exceed reserved throughput: our default behavior is to return a clear over-capacity response (HTTP 429) with guidance for retry/backoff (including a request id, and Retry-After where applicable), rather than queueing indefinitely and causing tail-latency spikes. We can also configure per-route limits/guardrails so a single hot route or runaway client can’t starve the rest of your traffic.

Attaching the current Dedicated SLA PDF and a short explainer on priority lanes terminology.

If you’d like, we can do a 20 min working session to map your expected peak/burst profile to (a) the reservation size and (b) the over-capacity behavior you want (fail-fast vs limited queueing for specific routes).

Best,
Lauren
